en: Catalog number: M00530 Uniform title: Sanatkumāra-tantra

Description: Vaiṣṇava tantra. Likely a late work, possibly of Bengali origin. It teaches a program of daily worship centered on the morning rites. Notes: Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: September 13, 2021. Publisher: Rasika Monana Caṭṭopādhyāya.
Publication year: Pre-1900 Publication city: Calcutta Publication country: India
The Sanatkumāra Tantra, Chapter One.
Oṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa;

salutations to the wielder of the discus, whose stainless yellow garment is like the golden filaments [of a lotus], and whose discus was rubbed against the shoulders of his great-armed enemies. || 1 ||
Then, in a secluded and delightful world frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
Pulastya bowed to Sanatkumāra and asked this.
You ought to recount the majesty of the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa; O you of noble vows, show me favor by explaining the King of Mantras according to the proper method.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, I shall describe the form of Kṛṣṇa as he performs his childhood deeds,
by whom I, along with the sun, Rudra, and Indra, am eternally held under control.
Or rather, O best of the twice-born, how can his greatness be described?
He is called Viṣṇu in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
I shall describe its ritual procedure according to the truth; listen attentively.
First, having received the mantra from the mouth of a guru, one should be endowed with devotion.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, one should perform the preliminary service (pūrvasevā),
having satisfied the twice-born with a joyful inner self.
Having first performed the occasional rite (naimittika) and worshipped the Sun with devotion,
and likewise having performed the worship of the deities, one who is endowed with compassion should perform the sacrifice (yāga).
On a mountain, by a river, in a forest, at a sacred ford, in a cow-pen, in a temple, or likewise at a holy fig tree or on the shore of the ocean, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times.
Having performed the hundredfold rite of the eightfold offerings and having eaten in the designated places, the wise man should worship Madhusūdana with the sixteen-fold service.

Having meditated at the proper time according to the rule, one should present the food offering (naivedya) to Viṣṇu; now listen to the king of mantras for the invocation by means of the heart-mantra. || 11 ||
Being composed and pure, the wise one, full of devotion, should extract [the mantra], first uttering the syllable *oṃ* three times for the Supreme Lord. (12)
Whatever desire the mantra-practitioner may have, he should announce it at the beginning of the mantra;
[he should visualize] a lotus-born [Brahmā], endowed with that face, situated above Śakra.
The first [syllable], endowed with a moon-drop and a crest, grants all desires;
it is a sacred ford mounted upon fire, established at the head by Śrī.
The second [form] is pervaded by the moon-drop crest and bestows prosperity;
it is Rudra, joined with a lotus, seated upon fire. || 15 ||

The third [letter], surmounted by the moon-drop (bindu) and the crest (śikhā), is considered to bestow liberation. [The letters] ending in *kha*, *na*, *cha*, *dha*, and *la*, along with the two moving ones (*ca* and *ja*), [are likewise]. 16.
The end of *vā*, the end of *mā*, likewise the end of *ṣā*, the end of *lā*, and the end of the end of *sā*; likewise *e-param*, *ai-param*, *apara-anta*, and the triad of *para*. (17)
One should first utter the word "gopījana," followed by "vallabhāya," and then give the word "svāhā"; thus complete, it bestows success.
Thus ends the first chapter in the work of Sanatkumāra. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter:
Now I shall correctly explain the ritual worship as well as meditation; listen to the meditation for the three periods of the day and the offering of food.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, having become pure and composed,
and having sat upon his seat, he then bowed to the Guru with palms joined in reverence.
One should repeatedly contemplate oneself as the form of Brahman;
having recited the mantra, one shall become victorious over all disputants.
Then, having bathed and become pure, the preceptor should perform the Vedic rites such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and likewise the worldly rites according to the instruction of his teacher.
Reciting the root mantra, "I satiate Śrī Kṛṣṇa," one should perform the libation;
then, having sat at the entrance of the shrine, the wise one should wash his feet.
The knower of mantras, having bound his topknot with the weapon-mantra and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), that best of practitioners should worship the deities of the doorway.
Having dispelled the obstacles and purified the hands and the ground,
one should bow to the Guru and Gaṇeśa, and then perform the worship of Vāstu.
Having worshipped Brahmā, thereafter [the practitioner] should occupy his own seat;
then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the wise one should contemplate "I am the Deity" within himself.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform all the Ṛṣi-nyāsas and so forth for the Mātṛkās; he should then perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the limb-assignment (aṅganyāsa).
The best of the twice-born [received] the Ācakra, the Sucakra, the Vicakra,
the Cakra for the protection of the three worlds, and the Asurāntaka.
Having placed each one starting from the east, one should apply the word "cakra";
having established it in the dative case, one should immediately follow it with the word "svāhā. (11)
Likewise, having uttered each limb [of the mantra], one should apply them individually:
*namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and likewise the weapon-mantra (*astrakam*).

The wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with his own powers, Keśava and the others, in due order upon the heart, the head, the crest-region, the body, and likewise in the directions.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the cage of manifestations (vibhūtipañjara), one should perform the placement of its forms (tanmūrtipañjara);
then the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) as well as the placement of the hands (karanyāsa).

One should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) in three ways; wherever there is the ten-syllable mantra, there one should perform the Vibhūtipañjara placement.
In this manner, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) as prescribed in the Kalpa, in their proper sequence;
furthermore, one should also perform the installation of the conch according to the instructions of the Guru.
Having likewise prepared the *arghya* and diligently sprinkled the ritual substances,
one should arrange the seat within one's own body and worship Dharma and the other [Tattvas].
And one should likewise worship Ananta and the others within the heart according to the prescribed rule;
for a householder, external worship is primary, whereas for those belonging to the [other] orders, internal worship is the main practice.
Having fashioned a yantra out of copper, one should arrange Ananta and the others;
in its corners, Dharma and the rest, and on its sides, the primary dharmas.
In the center as well, one should constantly worship the fourteen [deities] beginning with Ananta;
and in the filaments (keśaras), indeed, one should worship the deities beginning with Vimalā.
Having meditated upon oneself as the deity, one should draw [the deity] out through one's own nostril,
invoke him with effort, and worship the God.

One should perform the placement of the vital breath (prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā) using the seed-syllables beginning with "Ananta," and one should diligently worship the groups of forms (ākṛtīgaṇas) with water for the feet and other offerings.
Having brought incense and lamps, one should offer the food oblation (naivedya);
and having recited the mantra prescribed in the Tantra, one should personally worship [the deity] as if he were a god.
Having diligently recited the root mantra, "I satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa," one should offer libations three times with water from the arghya vessel into the center of the mantra.
The wise practitioner should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) and install the three pervading [mantras] according to the procedure prescribed in the Tantras. 25.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Sūtra of Worship," in the Sanatkumāra Tantra. || 2 ||

Now begins the third chapter. Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall explain in detail how the individual soul (jīva), together with its essential principles and joined with Kuṇḍalinī, [is to be extracted] by means of the Haṃsa-mantra.
One should unite [the mind] with the Supreme Brahman by means of the method joined with yoga;
one should contemplate the smoky seed-syllable of air (yaṃ) in the left nostril. || 2 ||
With his body thus purified, he should expel the wind through the right [nostril];
he should contemplate the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ) upon the right nostril-passage. || 3 ||
The fire generated by that [syllable] reduces his dry body to ashes;
he should then be sprinkled with the white-colored seed-syllable *Ṭhaṃ* by means of Vāmā.
Having placed [the mantra] on the forehead situated in the moon, one should then strike with it;
by that, the body produced becomes pure and very beautiful.
Having meditated according to the prescribed rite, one should lead the individual soul (jīva) to its own station—
[the soul] which is "I" (so'ham), surrounded by the mantra, the kuṇḍalinī, and the principles (tattvas).
This purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) has been declared, which bestows all prosperity;
now I shall describe the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), so listen attentively as it truly is.
One should exhale the breath through the *dakṣā* [nāḍī] with a measure of thirty-two *mātrās*,
and draw in the breath through the *iḍā* with a measure of sixteen *mātrās*.
Having placed [the mind] within the center of the *suṣumnā*, one should hold it for a duration equal to the number of the *vidyā*;
by the same [nostril] through which one fills the breath, one should exhale it again.
One should exhale by the same [nostril] through which one previously inhaled, and then fill [the breath] again by that same [nostril];
having placed [the mind] between the two, one should practice retention for their respective durations.
Next, I shall describe the previously mentioned form of that established prāṇāyāma along with the Mātṛkā-nyāsa; listen as it is correctly explained. (11)
On the forehead and on the face, as well as on the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the two cheeks, the two lips, and likewise on the two teeth; || 12 ||
One should place the vowels in sequence upon the head and the face,
and likewise on the hands, the feet, the joints, and the front, according to the prescribed rule.
On both sides, on the back, as well as at the navel and the belly,
one should place the letters beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', each situated in its respective location.
One who is free from disease should diligently perform the placement of the four letters beginning with *ya* in the heart, the two shoulders, and the two arms. (15)
And these six vowels alone are assigned to the heart and other locations; the determination of the hands, feet, navel, mouth, and lips is as follows. (16)
This indeed has been declared as the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, which bestows all prosperity.
Now I shall describe the Pīṭha-nyāsa; listen attentively as it truly is. (17)
One should arrange the recitation within one's own body in the sequence beginning with Dharma;
then one should worship Bhāskara, Gaṇeśāna, Śiva, and Durgā.
The wise preceptor, proceeding clockwise, should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the two shoulders and the two thighs in sequence: Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
One should visualize unrighteousness (adharma) and the other [qualities] at the mouth, the sides, and the sides of the navel;
dharma and the others are remembered as the feet, while the others are the limbs of the pedestal.
Within this lotus in the infinite heart, one should place the Sun, Moon, and Fire,
preceded by the syllables of the *praṇava*, along with their respective digits (*kalā*).
Likewise, the most excellent of the three gurus should assign the three qualities,
sattva and the others, as well as the Self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman).
The wise one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the self consisting of knowledge, preceded by the seed-syllable of Māyā;
he should utter "namo bhagavate" and then say the word "viṣṇave."
One should utter the word "sarvātmasaṃyoga" and the word "yogapadma";
ending with "pīṭhātmane" and preceded by "hr̥t," this mantra has been declared for you. (24)
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā are the Śaktis;
likewise, Brahmī, Īśā, and Īśānā are the Grahas, with Nandā considered the ninth.
On whatever seat one may be, one should perform worship upon that divine seat;
[the powers] Desire, Knowledge, and Action, as well as Kāminī and Kāmadāyinī.
Rati, Ratipriyā, and Manonmanī in the center—
such as I am, I shall take refuge in the corpse of Sadāśiva, ending with "ṅe," together with the Goddess.
Having thus performed the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), one should meditate upon the chosen deity.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Worship of the Pīṭhas," in the Sanatkumāra Tantra.
Now begins the fourth chapter:
Having meditated upon the Lord, who consists of the universe, who has the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, who holds butter in his right hand, and who is clad in yellow garments; || 1 ||
Having invoked [the deity], one should worship with mantras preceded by the ritual installation of the conch;
having sprinkled [the area] with water from the conch-mantra, [one should place the fire] to the left in the fire-mandala.

The wise one should place the common vessel and worship it according to the prescribed rite with waters consisting of nectar dripping from the *bindu*, along with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
One should meditate upon the support (ādhāra), fire (pāvaka), the conch (śaṅkha), the sun (sūrya), water (toya), and the moon (sudhākara);
one should contemplate the respective digits (kalās) of fire, sun, and moon in their proper sequence.
Having touched [the disciple], one who knows the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) should recite the root-mantra (mūlamantra) and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
having worshipped [him] thoroughly with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra), one should again cover him with both hands.
The preceptor, regarding himself as the deity, should recite the mantra at the proper time,
having protected [the area] with the weapon-mantra and veiled it with the armor-mantra.
Having formed the dhenumudrā, one should awaken it with one's own mudrā:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī! (7)
"O Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāverī, be present in these waters!
This is the mantra for the invocation of the sacred sites (tīrtha-āvāhana), declared to bestow all prosperity. (8)
Having taken the *prokṣaṇī* vessel filled with water to the south,
and having taken a small amount of the *arghya* water, one should pour it into the *prokṣaṇī* water.
To the north of the *arghya* vessel, the *pādya*, *arghya*, and *ācamanīya* vessels should be placed;
the Guru should sprinkle himself and all the sacrificial materials everywhere with water.
The ritual for the installation of the conch has been correctly described as bestowing all prosperity;
Śiva and the others are to be worshipped, as are the deities of the limbs within Keśava. 11.
Having invoked [the deity] with the *prāṇa-mantra*, one should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*).
At the end of the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa*, one should again utter the word "haṃsa" followed by the word "amuṣya" (of this one).

"Successively: 'The vital breaths here are the vital breaths,' and likewise, 'the individual soul (jīva) is situated here'; then for this [person], 'all the sense organs,' and again, one should utter the word 'of this'. (13)
Speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath—these limbs, having come here afterwards, may they remain long at the mouth; *ṭha* twice. (14)
This is declared to be the *prāṇamantra*, the bestower of life upon all. The Guru should first utter a greeting and inquire after their welfare. (15)
One should offer water for the feet (pādya) to the lotus-feet of the Lord with the heart-centered self;
this is said to be [performed] with śyāmāka, dūrvā grass, lotuses, and viṣṇukrāntā.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) into the mouth with the *svadhā* mantra;
this is stated by those who know the Tantras to be accompanied by *jātī*, cloves (*lavaṅga*), and *kakkola*.
Then the preceptor should offer the *arghya* upon the head with the *śiras-mantra*,
using scents, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, *kuśa* grass, water, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
This arghya for all the gods is declared to be made with dūrvā grass;
thereafter, being composed, one should offer the madhuparka with the *svadhā* mantra.
This mixture of clarified butter, curd, and honey has been declared by the wise;
thereafter, one should perform the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) with water, while identifying oneself with the *svadhā* essence.
One should cause a bath with scented water to be performed and have two garments donned;
one should also give a sacred thread along with necklaces and other ornaments.
Then, having sprinkled the Lord of Gods with the arghya water, one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings,
as prescribed with scents, sandalwood, camphor, and black agallochum.
Having worshipped with diligent effort using the sixteen types of offerings, you should worship the enclosures (āvṛtis) with devotion; listen attentively as I explain how this is to be done.
One should worship Vāsudeva and Devakī, as well as Nanda and Nandapriyā,
and likewise Kamalā, Bhāratī, Rati, and Śānta, upon the petals.
One should worship the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the kaustubha gem;
likewise, one should worship the śrīvatsa mark, the calf, and the forest garland.
Immediately after that, one should worship the Lord of Birds with the root mantra alone;
then, O God, one should worship the deity with his own seed-syllable, followed by perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
Then, one should recite the mantra with a lotus-seed rosary according to the prescribed number;
thereafter, one should worship the deity, followed immediately by the heart-mantra and the other limbs.
Having made one's own body [the vessel], one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
then, one should worship Viṣvaksena with the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of the Deity. || 28 ||
In this manner, the worship of Kṛṣṇa should be performed in sequence by those who are composed;
thereafter, having honored the cows, one should offer them a most beautiful morsel of food.
It was adorned with armlets, bracelets, necklaces, earrings, waist-bands, anklets, wild flowers, and various gems.
Then [he saw] the sky-dweller, stainless with the moon, planets, and stars, endowed with the luster of jewels, and adorned with every ornament. (31)
In the morning, one should worship Kṛṣṇa, who is endowed with all auspicious marks and is being praised by Sanaka and others stationed in celestial chariots in the sky.
Likewise, he saw him seated upon a jeweled throne within a golden pavilion in a forest endowed with the radiance of a kalpa-tree, surrounded by a hundred beautiful women.
One should meditate upon the beautiful Kṛṣṇa at midday, who increases the god of love, being fanned with yak-tail whisks and the like, and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum.
Standing in the midst of the hosts of cowherds and in the midst of hundreds of beautiful women,
he made them all subject to his own will and sported with them, filled with joy.
Adorned with perfumes, sandalwood paste, garlands, and other ornaments—a feast for the eyes—one should meditate upon the dark-eyed Lord at midnight just as one does at night. (36)
In a vessel of gold, silver, or copper— or even if such are unavailable—
one should worship Kṛṣṇa with devotion and offer the food offering (naivedya).
In the morning, one should offer rice cooked with curds, and likewise milk-rice thereafter;
similarly, one should offer beautiful milk with sugar at night. (38)
By serving the Supreme Lord through these very methods, the man who performs japa attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (39)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Sanatkumāra Tantra. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now I shall declare another mantra; listen attentively as it truly is.
I shall proclaim the body of the mantra, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
By the mere grasping of which a man becomes omniscient, and he shall obtain unshakable fortune and poetic skill esteemed throughout existence. (2)
The practitioner of mantra shall accomplish that which is unaccomplishable, even that which is difficult for the gods to attain.
O great sage, this secret heart-mantra of mine is what you should ask about. (3)
Mantras accomplished through other means all bestow their fruits;
even if a mantra has not been formally mastered, it will grant its fruit once it has been received.
For where the guru is satisfied, the Lord of the Universe is satisfied there;
having received the mantra, one should never doubt the word of the guru.
Taking refuge in the body of the Guru, the mantra-body abides;
therefore, one should worship the Guru with the mantra with one's entire being.
Having worshipped with perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps according to the guru-mantra,
one should then receive the mantra while covering the head with a cloth.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, consisting of gold or even a cow;
one should perform all the rites while avoiding stinginess regarding wealth.
O best of Brahmins, it is certain that an action performed without a sacrificial fee is in vain;
this was declared in the past by Viṣṇu himself, unwearied, to Nārada.
"Give me gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), along with a rosary and a water-pot;
then, O great sage, receive the mantra from me according to the prescribed rite. (10)
An action performed devoid of the prescribed rules does not bestow success at all.
[One should perform it] on a level, pure plot of ground smeared with cow dung. || 11 ||
Having established the conch there, one should place it within the form of the Mātṛkā;
beginning with the Supreme Brahman, one should extract the entire collection of phonemes.

One should extract the mantra ending in *svāhā*, consisting of the letters *sa* (the end of the *śānta* group), *ma* (the end of the *matha* group), *māṃ* (me), and *vahni* (fire), joined with the *vāma* (left) *trika* (triad) and the *bindu*; these three [groups] become a single syllable. || 13 ||
Then, having received it from the mouth of the Guru, one should fix it in one's heart;
having performed ten thousand recitations, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with senses subdued. || 14 ||
Being well-restrained, one should offer oblations into the fire ten times the [number of recitations], combined with the three sweets;
or else, being self-controlled, one should offer a thousand flowers dedicated to Viṣṇu.
And for the sake of attaining rubies, one should perform an additional thousand recitations;
it is taught that one should offer oblations amounting to a tenth part of that recitation, or twice as much.
O great sage, understand its reality as it is being carried forth:
for the root-syllable of Śambhu is established within it, as are the three powers.
Likewise, Brahmā, possessing the form of the moon-point (bindu), [is] at the end of the Śiva-mantra.
This, O child, has been told to you—the supreme heart-mantra.
Indeed, nothing should be told to anyone that is difficult to obtain within the three worlds;
for when the mantra has been thus accomplished, the three worlds are thereby mastered.
Having performed the ritual service (kāmya-karman), being pure and having conquered the senses, one should recite the mantra;
then, through action, mind, and speech, one shall accomplish whatever is desired.
That shall be swiftly accomplished for him, even if it be exceedingly difficult to achieve;
[for] Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, Durgā, and all the deities [are his protectors]. (21)
This mantra is a great mantra; it resides in the heart of all.
By reciting this mantra, one obtains double the fruit. || 22 ||
Now listen to how the worship of this mantra should be performed:
the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) are to be done with each syllable of the mantra.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus and having invoked the Lord with diligence,
one should then worship Gopāla either upon a sacrificial mound or in water.
And I shall now describe the meditation upon Gopāla, the teacher of the world:
he has matted hair, two arms, is naked, and possesses the luster of the petals of a blue lotus. (25)
The child Hari, about six months old, was crawling on his knees;
he was bound by a rope around his belly and tethered between two trees with a mortar.
And having come swiftly and effortlessly between the twin Arjuna trees, he playfully pulled the mortar sideways.
Having uprooted two trees a yojana in length with this mantra,
and having placed Vāsuki upon a rope, he bound him with this mantra.
[The Lord], laughing, dragged out and uprooted the two *yamalārjuna* trees, which were stuck fast in the mortar and entwined by the king of serpents. 29.
Surrounded by all the cowherds and cowherdesses who were crying out "Alas!
Alas!", Yaśodā came quickly and took him onto her lap as she wept.
Having thus reflected upon the Gopāla who consists of Māyā yet is free from affliction—the form of the entire world concealed by the guise of a cowherd—(he worshipped him). 31.
Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, one should complete the rite of recitation;
or otherwise, the worship of the Enemy of the Gods (Śiva) should be performed with these very same items.
One should offer incense, a lamp, food offerings, betel leaves, and so forth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the work of Sanatkumāra. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter: Having first uttered the word *kṛṣṇāya*, then *govindāya*, followed by the word *gopījana* at the end, and finally *vallabhāya* up to the *dviṭha* (svāhā). || 1 ||
The eighteen-syllable mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma, has been declared;
the mantra joined with eighteen phonemes has been explained according to the prescribed rule. (2)
The mantra of eighteen syllables begins with Śakti and Śrī; the one of twenty syllables consists of Smara, Kṛṣṇāya, and the pair of Ṭha-s (svāhā). Thus the six-syllable mantra has been declared. (3)

Having first uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ), the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) "Kṛṣṇa," followed by the word ending in "ḍe" (kṛṣṇāya), and then that same [mantra] for the Son of Devakī, conjoined with *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. || 4 ||
This sixteen-syllable mantra is proclaimed as belonging to Govinda;
thereafter, one goes for refuge to the glorious feet of Mukunda.
"I am pleased," thus was spoken; this is the Maukunda mantra of eighteen syllables.
It consists of the five-ending [letter] situated on the earth (D), adorned with the bindu (M), and is the Manu-mantra. (6)
This is declared to be the seed-mantra of the aggregate (piṇḍabīja), which bestows all accomplishments;
it consists of the aggregate and the seed of the Lord of Rati, followed by "namo bhagavate. (7)
To the son of Nanda, who possesses the body of a child and so forth, and who is dark-complexioned;
[the mantra] ends with the word "Vallabha" at the conclusion of the region of the Gopīs and concludes with the two Ṭha-sounds (svāhā). || 8 ||
The mantra of Gopāla, the Lord of the Universe, is declared to be in the Anuṣṭubh meter;
it is said to consist of six syllables, ending with "gopālāya agnijāyā" (gopālāya svāhā).
The two names Kṛṣṇa and Govinda ending in the suffix -aḥ constitute a seven-syllable mantra;
Śrī-śakti-māraḥ and Kṛṣṇāya-māraḥ are other seven-syllable [mantras]. || 10 ||

Klīṃ glauṃ śrīṃ, followed by "salutation to the dark-limbed one" (śyāmalāṅgāya), constitutes the ten-syllable mantra; with the addition of "the discus-bearer" (cakrī) and "the emanation of Vāmana" (vāmanasargau), it is known as the single-syllable mantra. || 11 ||
Kāma, Indra, Māyā, and Lavalāñchitamastaka—this is declared to be the single-syllable mantra of Kāma mentioned previously. || 12 ||
All of this—the word "Hṛṣīkeśa" ending in the dative case and the word "namaḥ"—is declared to be the eight-syllable mantra that resides in the hearts of all. (13)
Vāgbhava, the seed-syllable of Kāma, "Kṛṣṇāya," Surasundarī, Govinda joined with "ṅe," and immediately thereafter the seed-syllable of Ramā. (14)
Then follows the ten-syllable [mantra], and after that one's own seed-syllable;
this twenty-two-syllable mantra bestows all spiritual accomplishments. || 15 ||

KĀMAṂ MĀYĀṂ CA LAKṢMĪṂ CA DAŚĀRṆAṂ CA TATAḤ PARAM | TRAYODAŚĀRṆAMANTRAḤ AYAM PROKTAḤ SARVASAMṚDDHIDAḤ || 16 || This thirteen-syllable mantra, consisting of Kāma, Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Daśārṇa followed by that [the seed-syllable], is declared to bestow all prosperity.
"Grant me Kāma, Lakṣmī, and Māyā; grant the two feet of Jayakṛṣṇa!
Grant me Māyā, Lakṣmī, and likewise Kāma; grant victory, O two feet! (17)
The mantra is declared to consist of twenty-four syllables and end with "svāhā.
After that, one should add "kāmaṃ piṇḍaṃ tathā lakṣmīṃ gopālāya. (18)

"Lakṣmīm piṇḍam tathā kāmam govindāya padam tathā | kāmapiṇḍam tathā lakṣmīm svāhāntaḥ praṇavādikaḥ ||" (19) [The mantra is: Oṃ Lakṣmīm Piṇḍam Kāmam Govindāya Svāhā; likewise, Oṃ Kāmapiṇḍam Lakṣmīm Svāhā. It begins with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ends with Svāhā.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the [work] of Sanatkumāra. || 6 ||
Now begins the seventh chapter.
I shall describe the procedure for worship in due order; listen attentively as it is told.
Nārada is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas).
The deity has declared that Kṛṣṇa bestows the fruits of all desires;
[the mantra] consists of four syllables from the Vedas and six syllables from the pair of eyes, in sequence.
One who knows the mantras should perform the five limbs for the *manu*, excluding the *netṛ* (the seer).
For other mantras as well, the seers and the rest are the deities mentioned previously.
The limbs [of the mantra] consist of the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) joined with the eye (I) and long vowels;
for the ten-syllable [mantra], the Virāṭ meter is used, along with the five [limbs] beginning with ĀCakra.

The wise one of purified mind should perform the previously mentioned rites, such as the ritual placements (nyāsa), according to the prescribed rules; thus should he practice the meditation upon the Lord of the Universe.
One should remember Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, who incessantly enchants thousands of cowherd girls in the beautiful Vṛndāvana.
With the bees of their eyes directed toward the lotus-face of her own self,
and being tormented by the arrows of love, they longed for a prolonged embrace.
Bowed down by the weight of their full, high breasts shimmering with strings of pearls; with their hair-knots and garments loosened, and their ornaments slipping from the intoxication of passion.
Adorned with shimmering garlands of light emanating from their rows of teeth,
they gazed [at him] with various amorous gestures full of passionate pride.
With the luster of a full-blown blue lotus, a moon-like face, and a fondness for peacock-feather ornaments;
bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem, clad in beautiful yellow silk;
his body worshipped by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, surrounded by throngs of cows and cowherds—
I worship Govinda, who is intent on playing the melodious flute and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the eighteen-syllable mantra one hundred and five lakhs of times;
for others, one lakh, and for the ten-syllable mantra, ten lakhs.
One should first perform the preliminary service (pūrvasevā) according to the previously mentioned rule;
now hear the visualization (dhyāna) for the mantras of Bālagopāla according to the prescribed method.
The omnipresent Lord, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with lips like the ripe bimba fruit,
holds fresh butter and milk-rice in His two hands.
And likewise, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with one-tenth the number of recitations (japa),
using either clarified butter, fresh butter, curd, or milk-rice porridge.
The libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with Mallikā, Mālatī, and white lotus flowers, or with pure water, using one-tenth of that [amount]. || 15 ||
One should perform an ablution upon the head with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
and likewise feed Brāhmaṇas according to the sequence of the ten-fold portion.
Whenever a limb [of the ritual] should fail, the recitation (japa) must be twice that number;
when unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), the recitation is prescribed as four times the number of oblations.
For Brahmins and Kshatriyas, the quality is said to be eightfold;
for Vaishyas, it is eightfold; this is the rule for their women as well. (18)
Whatever caste a Śūdra relies upon, he should perform the service prescribed for that [caste];
for a Śūdra who relies upon a Vaiśya, it is recorded that the merit is tenfold.
This rule has been declared for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa); now learn it also regarding the libation (tarpaṇa).
In the libation, it is said to be twofold, and when one is capable, it is the means for accomplishing everything.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the determination of recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, from the *Sanatkumārīya*.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Now I shall declare the ritual applications; listen with proper attention.
One desiring irreproachable prosperity should perform oblations with *lakṣmī* flowers.
One should offer oblations of food mixed with clarified butter for the prosperity of that food;
one should honor Brahmins with wild flowers and kings with jasmine blossoms.
The practitioner of mantras should, in due order, bring under control Vaiśyas with white Campaka flowers, auspicious lotuses for Śūdras, and those of the three sweets (trimadhu) for all.
Having offered oblations in this manner, the best of the twice-born shall attain all his desires;
thereafter, with devotion, [he beholds] the dark-limbed one, the gracious Lord who is the glory of Gokula.

Having remembered the Lord who wears the attire of a child and is adorned with a garland of tinkling bells, the practitioner of mantra should satisfy him with auspicious waters, perceiving them as milk.
Having worshipped the God with *mālatī* flowers according to the prescribed rite, he joyfully bestows upon him wealth, grain, garments, and other such things.
One obtains long life, health, sovereignty, and the heart's desires;
one should offer oblations with Kāśa flowers one thousand and eight times.
By its mere name, all kings shall come under his control;
by offering oblations of ripe bilva fruits, one attains irreproachable prosperity.
Having offered a thousandfold quantity of jyotiṣmatī oil, he regains that very [woman] by means of full-blown red lotuses.
By this procedure, the practitioner becomes truly fortunate in the eyes of all; of this there is no doubt.
Through this rite, the mantra-master is liberated from great disease.
An oblation with fuel-sticks of the aśvattha tree brings back wealth that has been taken away;
by an oblation of dūrvā grass smeared with clarified butter, one is released from great danger.
He who recites ten thousand times the mantra of one's name ten thousand times shall become like that person's servant; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
What need is there for much speaking here? By means of this mantra, the excellent practitioner shall accomplish all desires, like another Viṣṇu manifest before his eyes. || 13 ||
A sonless man, having reached the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), should worship the Teacher of the World, saying:
"O Son of Devakī, O Govinda, O Vāsudeva, O Lord of the World! (14)
"O God, grant me a son; I have come to you for refuge.
Having praised him thus according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the groups of attendants.
First, the enclosures of the limbs are to be worshipped, followed by Dāma and the others;
then, in the cardinal directions, Dāma, Sudāma, Vasudāma, and Kiṅkiṇī.
Thereafter, one should worship Rukmiṇī and the other seven principal queens upon the petals;
they hold lotuses filled with nectar in their right hands, while their other hands are folded in mudrā.
Likewise, there were Rukmiṇī, Satyā, Nāgajitī, Sunandā, Mitravindā, Sulakṣaṇā, Ṛkṣajā, and Suśīlā. || 18 ||
Then, one should worship Vasudeva and Devakī, Nandagopa and Yaśodā, Balabhadra and Subhadrikā, at the tips of the petals.
The cowherds and cowherdesses, adorned with wonderful garlands and unguents, are to be worshipped;
these should be honored according to the prescribed rite, and immediately thereafter, Brahmā and the other deities.
Indra and the others are to be worshipped, followed by their weapons such as the thunderbolt;
then Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Varāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh, and Mahālakṣmī as the eighth—these are declared to be the Mothers of the Universe. || 22 ||
One should worship Indra and the others outside, together with their [respective] classes, weapons, and powers:
the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the goad. (23)
One should worship the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus right there;
having offered the food oblation according to the rules and meditated upon the God, the wise one should perform the recitation.
Having praised him and bowed with one's head, one should offer oneself with water;
first placing the word "itaḥ" (from here), and then the words "prāṇabuddhi" (life and intellect).

Now, regarding the states of waking and dreaming based on the functions of the body and the qualities [of the mind], as well as the state of deep sleep, [one should practice] through the mind, speech, and likewise through action. (26)
Whatever has been done with the two hands, with the feet, or with the belly, as well as what has been thought, what has been spoken, and likewise what has been performed by the penis; || 27 ||
Therefore, O Sundarī of the fire, let all that be an offering to Brahman;
may she properly surrender both me and everything belonging to me to Hari.
The mantra "Oṃ tat sat" is declared for the purpose of self-surrender;
one should worship the God every day with the sixteen types of ritual services (upacāras).
If one is unable to do that, there should be worship according to the local custom;
if one is unable even to do that, there should be worship with five ritual offerings.
A seat, a welcome, as well as the fivefold offerings beginning with water for the feet (pādya), bathing, clothing, ornaments, scents, flowers, and incense. || 31 ||
The lamp, the food offering (naivedya), and thereafter the handful of flowers;
the worship consisting of five services (pañcopacārikā) begins with fragrance and ends with the food offering.
Having offered the five [substances] beginning with *arghya* and likewise the five beginning with *gandha* according to their distinctions,
one should perform obeisance and the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*) rites according to the prescribed rule.
Having dismissed the deity from his heart, he should worship Viṣvaksena;
then, prostrating like a staff with both cheeks and the chin touching the ground.
With the nose, the head, the mind, and likewise with speech—this prostration with eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) bestows pleasure upon Hari. || 35 ||
All of this has been narrated by me both in sequential and non-sequential order; listen now to all that was not previously told, in its proper sequence. || 36 ||

Having performed the morning duties, one should perform the prostration, the bath, and one's own sandhyā rites; then the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of the purification of the elements up to the end of the *saṅkalpa* and the entire sequence of garlands;
the procedure for internal sacrifice, the external worship, and the installation of the conch and other vessels.
Then follows the worship of the pedestal, the sacrifice to the deities of the limbs, and the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). || 37 ||
Invocation, forming one's own mudrā, meditation on the Lord, worship, service, propitiation, incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings; the recitation [of mantras] in secret,
the offering of that recitation, the bearing of weapons, and thereafter the surrender of one's own self— [this is] praise.
And they obtain permission from the enemy of Mura; thus has the sequence of worship been proclaimed. || 38 ||
And this very Sūtra was proclaimed by him: "One should propitiate Acyuta";
thus was the Sūtra proclaimed of old by Nārāyaṇa himself. (39)
Formerly, this was revealed to me by Brahmā out of affection for me;
according to this rite taught by Pulastya, Kṛṣṇa has been worshipped by me.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Worship," from the *Sanatkumārīya*.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Pulastya said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, regarding that armor (kavaca) which has been revealed—"
O Lord, please out of compassion tell [me] that which is named the Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O best of Brahmins, I shall proclaim this most wonderful armor (kavaca),
which was formerly told out of compassion by Nārāyaṇa to Brahmā.
This supreme reality, the embodiment of the multitude of Brahma-mantras, which is most secret, was told to me by Brahmā; out of great affection, I shall speak it to you.
By wearing and reciting which, Brahmā unfailingly expands the creation;
by wearing and reciting which, Mahālakṣmī protects the three worlds. (4)
Through recitation and retention, Śambhu, the destroyer and knower of all principles, [is attained];
and Durgā, the mother of the three worlds, [slays] the great asuras such as Mahiṣa.
Since he slew the arrogant sons of Nara merely by reciting and retaining [this mantra],
so too may Indra and all others attain complete sovereignty.
One should reveal it to a disciple who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and a spiritual practitioner;
by giving it to a rogue or to the disciple of another, one shall meet with death.
Of this armor (kavaca) which is the auspiciousness of the three worlds, Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi),
the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Nārāyaṇa himself.
The application [of this mantra] is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
May the Praṇava protect my head, and may "namo nārāyaṇāya" protect it as well.
May the eight-syllable mantra protect the forehead and the pair of eyes, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
may *klīṃ* protect the pair of ears, and may the single-syllable mantra, which deludes all, protect them as well. (10)
Klīṃ, for Kṛṣṇa, [protect] my nose always; Govindāya, [protect] my tongue;
Gopījana-vallabhāya Svāhā, [protect] my body. 11.
May the eighteen-syllable mantra protect the neck, and may the ten-syllable mantra protect [the head].
May the mantra "gopījana-vallabhāya svāhā" protect both arms.
Klīṃ glīṃ klīṃ, "salutation to the dark-limbed one"—this ten-syllable mantra protects the shoulders.
Klīṃ kṛṣṇa klīṃ may protect the hands; klīṃ kṛṣṇāya may the one born from the limbs protect [the body]. 13.
May the heart-mantra *śrīṃ klīṃ bhuvaneśīṃ klīṃ* and *kṛṣṇāya klīṃ* always protect my two breasts; may [the mantra] ending with *gopālāya svāhā* always protect the pair of my flanks. (14)
May the supreme mantra *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* always protect the two sides;
may the mantra *smarādyau ṅeyutau* [namely] *kṛṣṇa-govindau* protect [the heart]. (15)
May the eight-syllabled mantra protect the navel; may the two-syllabled "Kṛṣṇa" protect the back; may "klīṃ kṛṣṇa kaṅkālam" protect the spine; and may "klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā" protect the skull.
May "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Kṛṣṇa Ṭha Ṭha" protect the two thighs constantly;
may the seven-syllable mantra protect the two shanks, and may the thirteen-syllable mantra protect them.
Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, followed by the word *padataḥ*, then *gopījanavallabhadaṃ*, and then *bhāyasvāhā*—this is indeed the anus-mantra consisting of ten syllables: *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. (18)
May the twelve-syllable mantra Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ always protect the knees;
may the thirteen-syllable mantra himself, whose weapon is the discus, protect the shanks.
May the powerful leader of Dvārakā, whose mantra consists of eighteen syllables beginning with *hrīṃ śrīṃ* and twenty syllables [in total], always protect all my limbs. 20.
"Obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, after that";
this twelve-syllable mantra beginning with "Tārā" shall always protect me in the east. (21)
May Viṣṇu, whose mantra consists of ten syllables— *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*— and sixteen syllables— *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*,
and who wields the mace and other weapons, protect me in the direction of Agni.
May the ten-syllable mantra, *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, always protect me on the right.
*Tāraḥ* (oṃ), *namo bhagavate rukmiṇīvallabhāya* (salutation to the Lord, the beloved of Rukmiṇī). || 23 ||
May this sixteen-syllable mantra, "svāhā," protect me in the southwestern direction;
may "klīṃ hṛṣīke padaṃśāya namaḥ" protect me in the western direction.
May this mantra of eighteen syllables, ending with *kāma* (klīm), protect me always in the northwest.
*Śrīṃ māyākāmakṛṣṇāya govindāya svāhā* is the mantra consisting of twenty-two syllables.
May Viṣṇu, residing in the twelve-syllabled mantra, always protect me from the north.
Then follows the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], "Kāmakṛṣṇāya," and thereafter "Hrīṃ Govindāya."
The twenty-two syllable mantra, "Śrīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā," may it always protect me in the northeast. (27)
I bow to the son of Devakī, the infallible King of Dance, upon whose central hood Kālī performs her divine dance.
May this twenty-two-syllable mantra also protect me from all sides below:
"We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon the one with flower-arrows. (29)
"May that Anaṅga impel us; may he protect me from above.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have described to you this [mantra] which embodies the multitude of Brahma-mantras.
The armor named Trailokyamaṅgala is of the nature of Brahman;
it was received from the mouths of Nārāyaṇa and Acyuta, the supreme lords headed by Brahmā and Īśa.
Out of affection for you, I have told this; it must not be spoken to anyone.
Then, having prostrated before the Guru according to the rules, one should recite the armor-verse (kavaca).
Even he who [teaches] once or twice according to his knowledge is a master of all mantras, consisting of all austerity; there is no doubt in this matter. || 33 ||

One hundred and eight recitations is prescribed as the procedure for its preliminary service (puraścaryā). Having performed the fire-oblations and other rites with a tenth part [of that number], one will certainly accomplish that goal. 34.
If one should possess the perfected armor, he would himself become Viṣṇu;
his mastery of the mantra would be achieved through the performance of the *puraścaryā* rite. || 35 ||
Having aroused a spirit of emulation, may Lakṣmī and Vāṇī dwell there forever;
having offered eight handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, one should recite [the hymn] once.
If one writes [this mantra] on birch bark, places it in a pill within gold, and wears it, one shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand years of worship. (37)
Whether on the neck or on the right arm, he too is Viṣṇu, without a doubt;
[it is equal to] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
Even those great gifts and likewise the circumambulation of the earth do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit from reciting this [name] just once. (39)
By the grace of the armor-mantra (kavaca), a man becomes liberated while living;
he truly agitates the three worlds and becomes a conqueror of the three worlds. || 40 ||
If one worships Puruṣottama without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca), the mantra will not grant success even if recited a hundred lakhs of times. || 41 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds," in the work of Sanatkumāra. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Pulastya said:
Within the context of the *karamālā*, let the rosary and the method of recitation (*japa*) be described.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O best of Brahmins, for I shall explain that rosary which was indeed asked about by you.
Beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger,
and starting from the little finger up to the base of the index finger, one should perform the recitation over the ten joints.
The index finger, the middle finger, and the little finger—
these three fingers shall have three joints each, while the middle finger shall have only one joint.
One should conceive of the first two as the central axis of Mount Meru;
the rosary is formed by the letters of the Mātṛkā, together with the bindu, arranged in both direct and reverse order.
In the rite of internal worship, one should employ the eight groups of consonants individually;
these eight groups are as follows: ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa-la. (5)
Listen now to those [beads] for the external sacrifice, such as lotus seeds and others:
rudrākṣa, conch, lotus seed, putrajīva, and pearls. (6)
The rosary of a householder should consist of twelve beads made of crystal, precious gems, gold, coral, or *kuśa* grass leaves. (7)
Counting on the fingers, it becomes eightfold when done with a line;
with *putrajīva* beads it is tenfold, and with conch shells it is a thousandfold.
That same [altar] made with coral and precious gems is known as the ten-thousand-fold;
when made with crystal, it is likewise declared, but with pearls, it is said to be a hundred-thousand-fold.
A rosary made of kuśa-grass knots yields a hundred million-fold merit, while a rosary made of rudrākṣas yields infinite merit;
likewise, a prayer garland fashioned from tulasī wood [is highly efficacious].
The rosary made of one hundred and eight beads, or fifty more, bestows the fruits of all desired objects for everyone; it accomplishes all rites. (11)
In the case of a recitation for universal purposes, it should be performed twenty-seven times;
one seeking liberation should recite twenty-five times, and one seeking wealth should recite three hundred times.
One seeking nourishment should use twenty-five beads, and fifteen for malevolent rites.
I shall now describe the stringing of the rosary as it was spoken by Brahmā in the past.
The garland should be like a cow’s tail, or it may take the form of a serpent;
one should join mouth to mouth and tail to tail.
O best of Brahmins, that very sūtra, whether fashioned by maidens or by women,
should be tripled and then tripled again, thus making it three times threefold.
White, red, black, or even silk thread should likewise be used for the rites of pacification, subjugation, malevolent magic, and even for killing. (16)
White, red, yellow, and black are the colors in sequence;
among all these colors, the red one grants all desired objects. (17)
Likewise, in the hermitages, one who is thus devoted obtains success in all things by worshipping Kṛṣṇa according to the tantras through the offering of fruits. (18)
The wise practitioner should recite each individual letter of the alphabet one hundred times;
then, taking the beads, he should string them onto the threads from the middle toward the tip.
Having thus formed the central knot and having strung the rosary with Meru knotted in the middle, one should then commence the consecration.
One should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra and with pure water;
one should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should fumigate it with the *aghora* mantra and gratify it with the *puruṣa* mantra;
one should consecrate each [item] individually, once by each of the five [mantras].
One should mentally consecrate Mount Meru once and [the mantra] a hundred times each;
one should then recite the mantra with that very same [consecration] by which the garland was established.
The wise man should not mutter any other mantra at any time; [he should recite]:
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta. (24)
"In every birth, in beginningless existence, worship me, the source of existence.
One should recite this in sequence, ending with the dative case, preceded by *praṇava* (OM), and concluding with *namaḥ*. 25.
Homage to Vāmadeva; homage to Jyeṣṭha; homage to Rudra; homage to Kāla; homage to Kalavikaraṇa; homage to Balapramathana. || 26 ||
To those who are non-terrible, to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the terrible—to all you Rudra-forms everywhere, obeisance to you! (27)
Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us. || 28 ||
Ishana, the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, the sovereign of Brahman, the supreme lord of Brahman—may Shiva be auspicious to me; may Sadashiva be auspicious to me.

Having consecrated the rosary in this manner with the great mantra beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "Sadāśiva" in due order, the wise one should then unite its vital breaths (prāṇas) therein.
The best of the twice-born should worship that rosary with the root mantra;
having fully honored the guru, he should receive the akṣamālā from his hand.
One should not touch [the vessel] with the left hand, nor should one allow it to fall from the hands;
the thumb is said to grant liberation, while the index finger destroys enemies. (32)
The middle finger brings about dense accomplishment; the ring finger is for rites of pacification;
the little finger is to be known for attraction; and [the thumb] bestows success in the rite of recitation. (33)
One should perform the circumambulation while standing with the foot placed between the joints of the big toe;
thereafter, being fully composed, one should personally perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
One should perform the *puraścaryā* having been initiated by the Guru himself, or by his own follower, or likewise by his brother’s sons, in all such cases.
Pulastya said:
What is the nature of the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and the procedure for the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) therein?
O Lord, please explain all of that in brief out of compassion. (36)

Sanatkumāra said: Having uttered the syllable *praṇava*, followed by *tat sat*, and also the month, fortnight, and lunar day, one should then recite the root mantra, saying, "I, so-and-so, of such-and-such a lineage. (37)
One who desires success in this mantra should recite it this many times;
thereafter, one should perform a fire-oblation (havana) consisting of a tenth part [of that number], and then a libation (tarpaṇa) consisting of a tenth part.
"One-tenth of that is sprinkling [with water], and one-tenth of that is feeding Brahmins;
indeed, I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa* in this manner, facing the northeast. (39)
Having thus resolved, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) and other rites;
and one should recite the mantra beginning at dawn until midday.
Having undertaken [the practice] according to such rules, one should perform the *puraścaryā*;
or else, the *puraścaraṇa* is described by another method.
During an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, being pure and having fasted beforehand, one should stand in a river flowing to the ocean with the water reaching up to the navel. || 42 ||
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra from the time of its reception until liberation;
having seen [the deity], bathed, and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should perform the recitation until the end of the liberation.
A pure man should perform recitation and other rites until the end of the lunar month;
through such recitation, the accomplishment of the mantra will surely occur—of this there is no doubt. (44)
If a man should abandon his recitation (jāpa) out of regard for ancestral rites (śrāddha) and the like,
he becomes an offender against the deity and leads seven generations of his ancestors to perdition.
I shall proclaim the duties of the month; listen attentively to that which was declared by Brahmā in ancient times for the sake of the purification of a devotee of Kṛṣṇa. 46.

I shall explain all of that succinctly and directly; listen, O Sage, regarding the conjunction of the full moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight under the asterism Phalgunī in the month of Phālguna.
Whoever swings Janārdana after honoring him with royal services [attains the merit] of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices. || 48 ||
A person who sees Kṛṣṇa swinging while facing the south attains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. || 49 ||
Those who keep a vigil before Kṛṣṇa while He is mounted on the swing are freed from heaps of offenses; of this there is no doubt. (50)
A person obtains the fruit of all merit in a mere moment;
therefore, I shall explain the procedure and what one should perform therein. (51)
On the full moon day, there shall be a great worship, and the Lord, together with the Saṅgha,
should be swung on a swing using either the thirteen-syllable or the eighteen-syllable mantra.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, worship should be performed according to the previously mentioned method;
having arisen, the mantra should be recited one thousand and eight times.
This sūtra has been proclaimed; listen to it from me in detail.
On the day of Revatī, the wise man should prepare the maṇḍala and the sacrificial offering for the site (vāstubali).
Having erected banners in all directions that possessed a splendor equal to that of the world-protectors,
[they placed] Govinda, the Lord of the Universe, upon a swing beneath a wooden platform.
One should worship with devotion according to the rules in the mandala, being composed in mind,
using the hymns of the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas, as well as the Puranic mantras.
With mantras belonging to the Āgamas and those of the Vaiṣṇava tradition, one should worship Hari;
and by extolling His virtues, the wise man should pass his time day and night.
He who performs dance and song before Keśava in the Kali age shall be liberated from thousands of offenses; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now describe another rite by which Viṣṇu is propitiated—the determination of the rules for installation as previously declared by Brahmā. (59)
Listen attentively to the account of the house of Lord Viṣṇu;
a pure temple was constructed there using grass and banners made of grass.
O best of men, he who gives this to Viṣṇu according to this rite shall certainly dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for a duration numbering hundreds of millions of years.
Whoever should give a variegated wooden temple to Vāsudeva shall dwell there for ten thousand yugas; this is declared as the truth.
That person who decorates [the temple] for Vāsudeva with various kinds of bricks shall dwell forever in the world of Viṣṇu for as many kalpas as there are bricks.
That man who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rites, should offer a variegated temple made of stone to Vāsudeva, is said to receive a hundredfold merit from that act.
Pulastya said:
O Lord, by what rite should a wise man offer a temple to Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of liberation? O Master, please describe this in due order.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having first offered the *vāstu-bali* sacrifice to the lords of the world (*lokeśa*) and the banners,
one should worship [the deities] together with their primary attendants (*mūla-pāriṣada*), using scents and other offerings according to the colors previously described.
One should worship [the deities] endowed with their respective signs, families, and lords, starting from the eastern direction in sequence;
one should worship the vajra and the other [emblems] in the tantra-vases with perfumes and so forth, in that same sequence.
To the east of that respective pavilion, one should construct the sacrificial hall (yāgamandira) on a site measuring one-third of its area, raised to the height of one cubit (aratni).
Having prepared the altar right there, one should draw the Sarvatobhadra [mandala];
and in the principal hall as well, the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
Having performed these rites, one should worship there with a concentrated mind at the archways:
Jaya, Vijaya, Vighneśa, and Kṣetranāyaka.
One should worship Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī in pairs, proceeding from the eastern direction in order, with offerings beginning with perfumes.
Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and incense,
one should then enter the house and worship the unborn Lord of the Site (Vāstveśa).
Then, one should sprinkle the maṇḍala with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water for the guest-offering (arghya);
having dispelled all obstacles right there, one should assume the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana).
One should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites according to the very procedure previously described;
then, having prepared the vessel for the offering water (arghyapātra), one should worship the pedestal (pīṭha) within the mandala.
There, the wise man should install an image known as Vāsudeva;
having propitiated the God upon the earthen lotus, he should worship Him with mental offerings of perfumes and other such items. (75)
Having drawn forth the vital energy from the path of the breath by means of the flower held in the hand,
one should project that energy into the image with the root mantra.
Placing the hand upon the heart, one should perform the installation of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa),
consisting of the seven letters beginning with *ya* and ending with the noose (*pāśa*) and goad (*aṅkuśa*), each accompanied by the nasal bindu.
One should utter "I" (ahaṃ) joined with the sky (viyat), truth (satya), and the moon (indu) in their entirety.
His vital breaths here are indeed the vital breaths; furthermore, his life-principle (jīva) is established here.
Having recited [the name] once more, one should again state all his sense organs;
then, for him as well, one should utter the words "speech, mind, eye, ear, and nose. (79)
"O vital breaths (prāṇas), having come here, may you remain happily for a long time—ṬHA twice.
Having thus established the vital breaths and invoked the Deity as before, and having formed the "tortoise-pose" with the hands, one should then meditate with undistracted mind. (80)
Viṣṇu, who resembles ten million autumnal moons, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus,
who dwells upon a white lotus, who deludes the world with his splendor,
and who is adorned with armlets, necklaces, earrings, a great crown, and shimmering bracelets— [I bow to him].
I salute Him who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem, and who is praised by the lords of sages. 81.
Having meditated thus, the wise one should recite the mantra with royal honors:
*Tāro hṛd bhagavān ḍentah vāsudevāya* thereafter. (82)
Among all the Viṣṇu-mantras, this mantra is declared to be the foremost;
with this mantra, one should cause all the offerings, beginning with the seat, to be presented. (83)
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the madhuparka, another sipping of water, a bath, garments, and ornaments. (84)
Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, water for sipping, as well as circumambulation, prostration, and dismissal—these constitute the sixteen [services]. (85)
Having entered the circle of shadows, one should worship Hari within the maṇḍala as before, and offer oblations into the consecrated fire according to the previous procedure.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with this mantra, the Vaiṣṇava should again worship before the deity and then worship the attendants.
The first rotation should consist of the [six] limbs; the next, of Vāsudeva and the others together with the powers such as Śānti; and the final one, of the twelve forms. (88)
The fourth [offering] is considered to be for the lords of the gods and others, and the fifth for Vajra and others;
when Viṣṇu is thus worshipped, he becomes pleased very quickly.
The heart-mantra is declared with *tāreṇa*, the head-mantra is uttered with *namasā*;
the crest-mantra is said to consist of four syllables, and the armor-mantra is considered to consist of five syllables.
The assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) for the weapon-mantra is said to be performed with the entire [mantra].
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—[these are the four forms]. (91)
These [deities] are four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
thereafter, a person should offer a temple with this mantra.
That meritorious soul, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, is indeed a god and not a mere human;
by doing this, he shall have fulfilled his purpose—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
One should chant the praises of the Abode with the hymns of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as with Smārta, Paurāṇika, Āgamika, and Vaiṣṇava mantras. (94)
Having offered a mirror, a chowrie, an umbrella, and a fan individually, one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with this mantra. 95.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, the best of the twice-born should then offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra of Gāyatrī, ending with "svāhā."
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should thereafter perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*);
having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests, one should feed the best of the twice-born.
By acting in this way, the meritorious soul becomes Nārāyaṇa in person.
In the giving of houses and other such gifts, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Śūdras—all are entitled to perform this. || 98 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Rosary," from the work of Sanatkumāra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Thereafter, I shall describe the limit of initiation; listen attentively as it truly is.
It consists of the Kriyāvatī, Kalāvatī, Varṇātmā, and Vedamātṛ [kalās].
In the initiation of the five āyatanas, which is the most excellent among all initiations, one abandons the names given by father and mother, as well as lifespan, caste, and complexion. (2)
The wise man, by means of the Saṃsṛṣṭi-mantra, should count them in order within the wheels:
Āṣāḍha, Nindita, Jyeṣṭha, Pauṣa, and likewise Bhādrapada.
Initiation is declared to be auspicious during blameless months and at the time of a lunar eclipse;
for the attainment of the goals of human existence, that disciple should take refuge with a guru.
Pure by birth on both his mother’s and father’s side, pure in disposition, and having conquered his senses,
he was a knower of the essence of all scriptures and a perceiver of the true meaning of all treatises.
Devoted to helping others, dedicated to worship and the recitation of mantras, his word was never in vain; he was peaceful and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
A human being becomes a guru when endowed with qualities such as these: following the path of yoga and being one who reaches the heart of the deity. || 7 ||
The disciple is of noble birth, pure in soul, devoted to the goals of human life,
one who has studied the Vedas, skillful, and who has cast far away the god of love.
He was always a well-wisher of living beings, a believer who had abandoned atheism,
constantly devoted to his own duty, and ever intent on the welfare of his father and mother.
Diligent in serving the guru through actions of speech, mind, and body—one endowed with these very qualities is a disciple, and no other. || 10 ||
O best of Brahmins, listen attentively to those very days within the twelve months which bestow auspiciousness. (11)

The thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, and the fifth day of Āṣāḍha known as Nāgapañcamī. (12)
The twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the eighth day of Bhādrapada conjoined with Rohiṇī,
and the highly meritorious Mahāṣṭamī in Āśvina bestow all desired boons.
The full moon of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, likewise the sixth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight in Mārgaśīrṣa, and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Pauṣa and Māgha. (14)
The determination of the time is as follows: the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna;
listen, O wise one, for these meritorious lunar days are praised as bestowing success. (15)
The fifth, seventh, sixth, and likewise the full moon day of the bright fortnight, as well as the thirteenth and tenth, are praised for all ritual acts. (16)
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), whether bright or dark, is praised and proclaimed as auspicious by the wise; likewise are the asterisms Aśvinī, Śravaṇā, Ārdrā, Revatī, and the three Uttarās. (17)
The auspicious Śatabhiṣā is likewise proclaimed for initiations and other rites;
now I shall explain the yogas for the benefit of practitioners. (18)
Those expert in yoga declare that yoga is the unity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman); others know it as the realization of the non-difference between Śiva and the Self. (19)
They say that desire and anger, greed and delusion, as well as pride and envy—these are the poisons; they are the perilous obstacles of the self. (20)
One should draw in the external air through the *iḍā* for sixteen measures;
one should slowly retain the air in the middle [channel] with the *vidyā* measure. (21)
The best among those who know yoga should expel this [air] through the piṅgalā channel;
those expert in the yoga scriptures call this prāṇāyāma. || 22 ||
Having repeatedly approached it, one should practice through constant repetition;
that Sanatkumāra-tantra originated from the preeminent sage.
He who reads or even hears this essence of the tantras from Sanatkumāra, which arises from the contemplation of Brahman, is also the best among the meritorious. (24)
In whosever house this written book remains constantly, Lakṣmī herself does not abandon that house during the three periods of the day. (25)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of Śrī Gopāla," in the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Pulastya within the *Sanatkumāra-tantra*.
